newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian leaders back German military role - Ruehe.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian leaders back German military role - Ruehe.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Wednesday his country's new military role in a NATO-led peace force enjoyed full support from Bosnian political leaders.
"All of them expressed that the German soldiers are very welcome in their new role in SFOR in Bosnia," Ruehe said after meeting Moslem, Croat and Serb members of Bosnia's peacetime government.

Ruehe told reporters that even Bosnian Serb representatives, who in the past accused Germany of siding with their Moslem and Croat foes, said they backed Germany's contribution of 2,000 troops to the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
The defence minister flew to the capital Sarajevo to inspect German troops as they formally launched their peacekeeping mission in a ceremony held in a barracks once used by the Yugoslav army.
The arrival of the 2,000-strong contingent this month marks the first deployment abroad of German troops from combat formations since World War Two.
The presence of German soldiers has so far sparked no angry reaction among the former warring factions despite bitter memories of atrocities committed during the Nazi occupation of old Yugoslavia.

Equipped with armoured personnel carriers and reconnaissance vehicles, the soldiers are drawn from a Franco-German brigade in Germany and will work under French command in the southwest near the town of Mostar.
Although they will be based in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, patrolling duties will bring the Germans into Serb-controlled territory as well, NATO officers said.

Ruehe, who led a delegation from the German parliament's defence committee, said Bosnian political leaders viewed military cooperation between France and Germany as an important example of reconciliation for their own country.

"In my talks I got the feeling that it was also understood that the integration between German and French soldiers has more than just a military meaning but has a very deep political meaning," Ruehe said.
"For all of us who have taken this difficult decision in the Bundestag, it is gratifying to see that it is understood in the right way what this contribution of Germany means."
He said members of the inter-ethnic government appealed to Germany to move cautiously with the repatriation of hundreds of thousands of Bosnian refugees who had fled the 43-month conflict.
Ruehe also met defence officials from the Moslem-Croat federation to discuss a German offer to train helicopter pilots, technicians and medical teams in the federation military.
The proposal was separate from the U.S. "train and equip" military aid programme and was meant to help with efforts to merge Moslem and Croat armies into a single force, Ruehe said.
Apart from the 2,000 soldiers serving in Bosnia itself, Germany has contributed another 1,000 airmen, sailors and other troops to the NATO-led force in former Yugoslavia.
Some 31,000 troops from the NATO alliance and other countries are policing the Dayton peace agreement in Bosnia in an 18-month mission due to expire in mid-1998.
